chapter.title: Across the pool, and staying safe

cards.body:
When you're tired in the middle of the pool, you don't have to race for the wall. You can rest on your back.

The bed doesn't stop at the edges. It's under you in every square metre of the pool, so **a rest is always one roll away**. Today you join every move into one trip across, and you learn to lie down whenever you need to.
cards.simpler: When you get tired in the middle of the pool, you don't have to hurry to the wall. You can rest on your back. Think of the water as a bed that doesn't stop at the edges. It is under you everywhere in the pool, so **a rest is always one roll away**. Today you put every move together into one trip across. You also learn to lie down on your back whenever you need to.

cards.prompt: You're halfway across, 6 metres from both walls, with no noodle in sight. Which of these lets you rest right where you are, holding nothing?

options.text: Lie face down, hold your breath and keep still

whyNot.a: That's treading water, not resting: your arms and legs keep working the whole time.
whyNot.c: That's the front float, not a rest: it holds you up, but you can't breathe in, so it only lasts a few seconds.

cards.reteach: A rest has to let you breathe and stop moving, both at once. On your back, your face stays out and the water does the holding, anywhere in the pool.

cards.title: Joining it up
cards.body:
Crossing the pool is four things you already know, in a row: push off and glide, start the kick, add the arms, and breathe when you need to. Slow wins. Ten calm strokes beat twenty frantic ones.

Around the middle, most beginners run out of breath before they run out of strength. So **turn onto your back**: drop one shoulder, roll, ears in the water, hips up, chest full of air. It's your day-3 back float.

Lifting your head high to gulp air doesn't work. Your head goes up like one end of a seesaw, your legs go down, and you end up half standing in the water you're trying to cross.
cards.simpler: Crossing is four things you already know: push off and glide, kick, add arms, and breathe when needed. Ten calm strokes beat twenty rushed ones. Around the middle, most beginners run out of breath before strength. So **turn onto your back**: drop a shoulder, roll, ears in, hips up, chest full of air, like your day-3 float. Don't lift your head to gulp air. Like a seesaw, head up means legs down, and you end up half standing.

cards.title: Priya's 12 metres
cards.body: Priya's pool is 12 metres wide. On her first full crossing she pushes off, glides, kicks, and at stroke 7 she runs out of breath, 6 metres from either wall. She **rolls onto her back** and stares at the ceiling: two broken lights and a faded banner for aqua aerobics. Five slow breaths later she rolls back over, finishes in 6 more strokes, and touches the far wall with breath to spare.
cards.simpler: Priya's pool is 12 metres wide. On her first full crossing she pushes off, glides, and kicks. At stroke 7 she runs out of breath, 6 metres from either wall. So she **rolls onto her back** and looks up at the ceiling: two broken lights and an old aqua aerobics banner. After five slow breaths she rolls back over. Six more strokes, and she touches the far wall with breath left over.

cards.prompt: Sam is 5 metres into an 11-metre crossing, in chest-deep water, and swallows a mouthful. Coughing starts. Which move fits this chapter?

options.text: Head up, paddle hard for the nearest wall
Put the feet down, stand, cough it out, then carry on
Swim faster to finish before the cough gets worse

whyNot.a: That's the seesaw, not a rest: paddling with your head up sinks your legs and costs breath you need for coughing.
whyNot.c: That's pushing through, not resting: going faster uses up breath you're already short of.

cards.reteach: In standing depth, your feet are your backup. Stand, cough with your head up, and wait until your breathing settles. Then swim on.

cards.title: Your backup
cards.body:
The roll is your rest. **Standing depth and someone watching are your backup.** So check the depth markings on the pool edge before you set off, swim with a friend or a lifeguard there, and get in by the steps.

If you're just tired, roll onto your back. If something goes wrong, like a mouthful of water, put your feet down and stand first.
cards.simpler: The roll is your rest. **Water you can stand in, and someone watching, are your backup.** So check the depth signs on the pool edge first, swim with a friend or a lifeguard there, and get in by the steps. If you're just tired, roll onto your back. If something goes wrong, like swallowing water, put your feet down and stand up first.

cards.body: Tom is 3 metres from the far wall and tired. He lifts his head to check how close it is, sinks a little, kicks hard, then lifts again to check. By the third look he's standing up and spluttering, 2 metres short. The sign to watch for: if you're **looking at the wall more than the pool floor**, roll over and rest first.
cards.simpler: Tom is 3 metres from the far wall and tired. He lifts his head to see how close it is, sinks a bit, kicks hard, then lifts it again to check. By the third look he is standing up and coughing, 2 metres short. Here is the warning sign: if you are **looking at the wall more than the pool floor**, roll over and rest first.

cards.prompt: A friend asks why you'd rest on your back in the middle of the pool instead of just heading for the wall. Best answer?

options.text: My back float comes with me everywhere, and resting on it lets my breathing settle
The wall is always further away than it looks, so never swim towards it
On my back I can kick harder and get there sooner

whyNot.b: That's about distance, not the reason: reaching the wall is fine, just not by using up your last breath sprinting.
whyNot.c: That's the kick from chapter 5, not resting: the back float works because you stop working.

cards.reteach: The wall stays in one place. Your back float goes wherever you go. Lying on it lets you breathe freely while the water holds you up, so you get your breath back, and after that the wall is easy.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Swimming across is push, glide, kick, arms, and a breath when you need one, all done slowly. When you're tired, **roll onto your back** and let the water hold you. Your backup is water you can stand in, with someone there.

Next: breathing to the side, the trick that turns a width into a full 25-metre length.
cards.simpler: Swimming across is push, glide, kick, arms, and a breath when you need one, all done slowly. When you get tired, **roll onto your back** and let the water hold you up. Your backup is water you can stand in, with someone there. Next comes breathing to the side, the trick that turns one width into a full 25-metre length.

cards.body: Next time you're at the pool, in chest-deep water: swim 4 strokes, roll onto your back, float for 5 slow breaths, then tuck your knees and stand. Do it 3 times.
cards.simpler: Next time you're at the pool, go to water that comes up to your chest. Swim 4 strokes. Then **roll onto your back** and float there for 5 slow breaths. After that, pull your knees in toward your chest and stand up. Do the whole thing 3 times.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now swim slowly across the pool, roll onto your back to rest when tired, and stand up when something goes wrong.

dubious_claims: Sam exercise: telling a coughing swimmer in chest-deep water to roll onto their back before standing is questionable safety advice. Standing up is the safer first move, and lying back while coughing risks taking in more water.
Card 1: 'the wall is not your safest option, your back is' conflicts with the chapter's own rule to stay where you can stand. In standing depth, putting your feet down is the safest option.

Exercise cards 2 and 5: counting prompt, options, both wrong-answer notes and the reteach, they come to about 126 and 133 words. That breaks the 120-word limit if the whole card counts. I passed short_cards only because a reader sees one note at a time.
repairedFrom.why: The four-habits card is a bolted-on checklist that no exercise tests, so the chapter teaches two things. Its 'stay where you can stand' rule also undercuts the hook: if you can stand, standing beats rolling onto your back.
repairedFrom.fix: Shrink the four habits to one line tied to the roll ('the roll is your rest; standing depth and a watcher are your backup'), and rewrite the Sam exercise so the right answer is 'stand up, cough, then carry on', which tests that line.
